comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
**Decided: the numbers name panes, they are positional, and the sidebar
order is yours to rearrange.** Tab numbering goes away in the same pass -
two numberings in one sidebar is worse than either.

**Positional, despite the doubt above, because rearrangement changes what
positional means.** The description worries that positions shift under
you, and that worry is about *involuntary* renumbering: a pane closes two
rows up and the number you read a moment ago now lands somewhere else.
An order you arranged yourself is not that. ⌘4 moving because you moved
the row is the behaviour you asked for, and stable allocation would fight
it - you would drag a row to the top and it would keep the number it had.

So the choice the description frames as positional-or-stable resolves
once the list is user-owned, and it resolves toward reading the number
off the row rather than remembering it.

**What a drag does is the open question, and it decides the size of this
card.** Two shapes:

- **It moves the pane in the window.** herdr has `pane.swap`, so the
  sidebar stays a faithful view of the tree, `view = f(daemon state)`
  holds, and nothing new is persisted. The constraint is that you get
  swap rather than arbitrary insertion, which is fine - reordering a tree
  is not otherwise well defined.
- **It is presentation only,** stored in `window.toml` beside tab order
  and widths. Free-form reordering, at the cost of a sidebar that no
  longer tells you where a pane is on screen, and of Muster owning an
  ordering the daemon has never heard of.

**Lean: the first.** Dragging an agent in the list and watching it move
in the window is a better feature than a list that disagrees with the
window, and it costs no new truth.

**One residue, worth naming rather than solving here.** Closing a pane
still shifts every number below it, so a number that reached you a moment
ago can be stale by the time you press it. That is not fixable in the
numbering, and the answer is elsewhere: a notification should name the
agent, not the chord. Relevant to a_28Q5b3oPA.

**Deferred, but keep it in mind.** Past nine or ten panes the numbers run
out and reaching a *specific* tab becomes useful again. `next_tab` and
`previous_tab` still cover browsing, so what would be missing is only the
direct jump - a second chord family, decided when the pane count makes it
bite rather than now.

creator: Alexander Terp
description:
Today ⌘1-⌘9 name **tabs**, via `RosterTab.place` - one numbering across
every attached daemon, drawn beside the tab caption in the sidebar. There
is no chord that goes to a named pane at all: panes are reached by
direction, by `next_pane`, or by clicking a row (a_28Nb8xJyb). Wanting to
jump straight to a specific agent is a gap, and the question is whether
to fill it by adding a second numbering or by moving the one we have.

**Lean: move it. The numbers should name panes.** Three reasons, in
increasing order of weight:

1. **The sidebar already disagrees with itself.** The rows that carry the
   state dots - the whole point of the product - are pane rows, and the
   numbers are drawn one level up, beside the captions. The eye lands on
   the dot and the number is somewhere else. That mismatch is what
   prompted this card.
2. **Numbering panes subsumes reaching tabs.** The stated reason numbers
   sit on tabs is that a tab is otherwise unreachable once the agent list
   is put away. But focusing a pane in a tab nothing is showing brings
   that tab on screen by definition - so pane numbers reach every tab
   too, through any pane in it, and the argument dissolves. The tab axis
   keeps `next_tab` and `previous_tab`, which is what it is for.
3. **The unit of this product is the agent, and an agent is a pane.**
   "Attention routing" promises that when an agent needs you, one
   keystroke lands you on *the pane that asked*. Today no keystroke does
   that - only a click does.

Costs, stated honestly rather than argued away:

- **Nine chords, fifteen panes.** The target is a window of fifteen
  agents. Tabs are fewer than panes, so nine numbers cover a larger share
  of them; moving to panes means ⌘1-9 reaches the first nine and the rest
  need `next_pane` or the mouse. The current scheme has the same ceiling
  (the sidebar already draws no number past nine) - it just bites later.
- **Panes churn faster than tabs.** `place` is positional, and its own
  doc comment already concedes "a number is a position, and positions
  shift". A tab list shifts rarely; a pane list shifts on every split and
  every close, which is muscle memory breaking mid-session.

That second cost is the real open question, and it is worth deciding
rather than inheriting: **positional or stable?**

- **Positional** - count down the sidebar - is what tabs do now. It reads
  off the screen with no memory, and it renumbers under you.
- **Stable** - a number assigned when a pane appears, kept until it dies -
  survives a split three rows above it, at the cost of gaps and of no
  longer matching "count down the list".

Tabs got positional and it is fine, because tabs churn slowly. Panes do
not, so the choice may not carry over, and this is the card to make it
on.

Two consequences to handle rather than discover:

- `focus_tab_1` through `focus_tab_9` would be lying about what they do.
  Rename to something the config file can say honestly; a `[keymap]`
  naming the old ones should fail loudly rather than silently do
  something else. Pre-alpha, so a rename is cheap now and expensive
  later.
- The tab captions lose their numbers and the pane rows gain them, which
  is a simpler sidebar than the one that draws both. Whatever is
  numbered, only one thing should be - "three ways to reach a tab cannot
  disagree" was the rule that shaped the current scheme, and it applies
  just as much to the replacement.
title: 🔢 The numbered chords name panes, and the sidebar is yours to arrange
